title: Mental Health Is a Warfighting Readiness Problem for the U.S. Navy
gist: Naval War College professor Heath 'Hank' Brightman argues the U.S. Navy's mental-health infrastructure — both ashore and at sea — is severely under-resourced relative to sustained combat operations against the Houthis and in a hypothetical China conflict, citing the USS Abraham Lincoln's early redeployment after a sailor's suicide attempt, a regulatory bottleneck barring the fastest-growing class of counselors from TRICARE work, and only 42 deployed 'triad of care' billets fleet-wide, and proposes a $3.8 million/year, 250-member civilian auxiliary corps plus university grant program as fixes.

insights.claim: The Navy redeployed the USS Abraham Lincoln following a sailor's purported deliberate attempt to go overboard, amid reports that the crew was 'struggling with exhaustion and declining morale, including reports of suicidal thoughts.'
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: A concrete, named operational readiness failure directly tied to crew mental health, used by the author as the flagship evidence that current Navy mental-health support is inadequate for sustained combat operations.
insights.quote: struggling with exhaustion and declining morale, including reports of suicidal thoughts

insights.claim: Among the crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln, almost half complained that they were not receiving adequate help coping with stress at sea, despite Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle's stated push for greater sailor connectedness and trust with leadership.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: Direct survey-level evidence of a mental-health support gap on a combat-deployed carrier, undercutting Navy leadership's public resilience messaging.
insights.quote: almost half complained that they were not receiving adequate help in coping with stress at sea

insights.claim: Only two 'triads of care' (embarked psychiatrists/psychologists, civilian resilience counselors, and chaplains) are currently underway in combat operations, aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln and USS George H.W. Bush, both in the Middle East, with a third aboard the USS George Washington transiting the Strait of Malacca to relieve the Lincoln.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: Quantifies just how thin at-sea mental-health coverage is across the deployed fleet during active combat operations (Operation Prosperity Guardian, Operation Epic Fury).

insights.claim: The Navy has about 42 deployed resilience counselor billets fleet-wide, roughly two per amphibious ship and carrier — a structurally thin at-sea 'triad of care' staffing level relative to the size of the fleet.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: A specific staffing-ratio benchmark (42 billets fleet-wide) that quantifies the scale of the shortfall the author is arguing needs to be addressed before large-scale combat operations against China.

insights.claim: Neurobiological research cited by the author suggests combat trauma correlates with reduced executive functioning (loss of sustained focus, degraded decision-making, impaired long-term planning), and that unless treated within six months of exposure, this degradation may persist for years.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: Establishes a specific, actionable clinical treatment window (six months post-trauma) that frames delayed mental-health access as a direct, lasting warfighting-capability degrader, not just a welfare issue.

insights.claim: Military OneSource providers are currently prohibited by Department of Defense policy from engaging in trauma-recovery work with service members, forcing most clients toward the more constrained TRICARE provider pool instead.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, named, and reversible DoD policy (the Military OneSource trauma-work restriction) as a primary chokepoint the author says could be removed to 'almost immediately' expand shore-based preventative mental-health care.

insights.claim: About 60 percent of TRICARE-eligible therapists are licensed independent clinical social workers (roughly 2,100 registered with Star Behavioral Health Providers), while the remaining 40 percent (about 1,140 clinicians) are licensed professional/mental health counselors, marriage and family therapists, and similar professionals — and only the latter group faces the accreditation bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: Precisely sizes the TRICARE provider pool split and identifies which sub-segment (mental health counselors) is being structurally excluded, sharpening the specific policy fix needed.

insights.claim: TRICARE providers must be graduates of programs certified by the Council for Accreditation of Counseling and Related Educational Programs, but such accredited programs are scarce near major Navy fleet concentration areas: Norfolk graduates only 4.2 percent of accredited-eligible mental health licensure candidates nationally, Mayport 3.7 percent, San Diego 2.6 percent, Puget Sound 1.3 percent, and Hawaii has zero accredited programs.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: A precise geographic mapping of the mental-health provider supply gap against the Navy's actual fleet concentration areas, useful for evaluating whether proposed university-grant fixes are correctly targeted.

insights.claim: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows employment of mental health counselors is projected to grow 17 percent from 2024 to 2034, versus only 6 percent for social workers over the same period — meaning the fastest-growing provider category is precisely the one currently blocked from full TRICARE eligibility by the accreditation rule.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: Highlights a policy mismatch: labor-market growth is concentrated in the credential category the Navy's current rules under-utilize, implying an easy structural fix (loosening TRICARE credentialing) would align policy with existing workforce trends.

insights.claim: Brightman proposes a pilot program providing $250,000 to $500,000 in support grants to each university located in a major fleet concentration area, to expand accredited counseling program availability and grow the pipeline of TRICARE-eligible counselors.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: A specifically costed policy proposal ($250k-$500k per university) that could be tracked for Navy or Department of Defense budget adoption.

insights.claim: The author proposes creating a 250-member civilian disaster resilience auxiliary corps, modeled on the Navy's Inactive Ready Reserve and the Air Force's Civil Air Patrol, that could become operational in 18 to 24 months and would reinforce at-sea triads of care during major combat operations, with members receiving a stipend of up to $5,000 per year during peacetime and legal protections (comparable to USERRA) upon activation.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: A concrete, modeled institutional proposal (250-person auxiliary corps) with a defined stand-up timeline (18-24 months) that could become an actual Navy program to track for implementation or funding.

insights.claim: Estimated startup costs for the proposed 250-member auxiliary corps are approximately $3.8 million per year, comprising roughly $1.6 million for large-scale-combat-operations simulation training and $1 million for travel and overhead, in addition to member stipends.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: A specific, low dollar-figure ($3.8M/year) policy ask relative to Navy budget scale, useful for gauging how cheaply this readiness gap could plausibly be closed if adopted.

insights.claim: The author cites the Navy's recently introduced Navy Reserve Innovation Unit — staffed by Fortune 500-level executives serving as hands-on experts on distributed teams — as precedent for the feasibility of a similarly structured civilian auxiliary corps for deployed mental-health support.
insights.speaker: Heath “Hank” Brightman
insights.so_what: Points to an existing Navy organizational model (Navy Reserve Innovation Unit) as a template being reused across multiple current Navy reform proposals, worth watching as a recurring institutional design pattern.
